text: Introduction
Research Context

The digitalisation of society has created an increasing demand for secure and trustworthy data sharing across organisational boundaries. Modern digital ecosystems involve multiple independent stakeholders, including individuals, healthcare providers, regulatory authorities, researchers, and third-party data processors [6, 19, 26]. The increasing digitisation of healthcare information enables patients, healthcare professionals, guardians, researchers, and healthcare organisations to participate in data-sharing processes [31, 21]. Healthcare data is highly sensitive and subject to strict privacy and governance requirements. Its exchange therefore raises complex questions concerning identity, authority, patient consent, privacy protection, accountability, and fine-grained access control [24, 22, 12, 25].

text: Traditional access-control architectures are based on centralised identity providers, institution-specific authentication systems, and relatively static permission-management mechanisms [28, 25]. These approaches can provide effective access control within an organisational boundary, but they become difficult to apply when authorisation decisions involve multiple independent entities. This problem is particularly relevant in healthcare, where data-sharing decisions may require the coordinated participation of patients, guardians, healthcare professionals, and institutional authorities [31, 9]. These scenarios demonstrate that authorisation is increasingly a distributed governance problem rather than simply a process of authenticating a user and checking a static permission [29].

text: Blockchain-based mechanisms can provide tamper-resistant recording and distributed auditability [1, 26, 8, 18], while decentralised identifiers can support the identification of participants without relying exclusively on a central identity provider. Verifiable credentials can provide cryptographically verifiable evidence concerning roles or authority [20, 5], and policy-based access-control mechanisms can restrict access to authorised resources [2, 28, 25]. However, an immutable record does not necessarily demonstrate that the participating entities were legitimate, that they possessed the required authority, or that a subsequent data-access request remains consistent with the conditions originally authorised. This requires a transition from viewing consent as a static record of permission towards understanding consent as an active and evaluable component of a broader authorisation process, extending the dynamic consent perspective [13, 24].

text: Problem Statement

Existing consent-management and decentralised access-control approaches represent authorisation through database records, access-control entries, smart contracts, or blockchain transactions. These mechanisms can improve integrity, traceability, and auditability, but consent often remains a passive artefact [10, 13]. The relationship between the consent record, the identity of the participants, their authority to act, the applicable policy constraints, and the resulting access decision is frequently treated as separate technical concerns. Likewise, successful authentication establishes that an entity has been identified, but authentication does not automatically establish that the entity possesses the authority to access a particular patient's information. Even where identity and collective approval have been satisfied, an access request may still be inappropriate if it exceeds the authorised purpose or data scope.

text: Research Motivation

The motivation of this research is to develop a Trust Computing perspective in which trustworthy healthcare data access emerges from the coordinated verification and enforcement of multiple security conditions. Under this perspective, trust is not treated as a property provided by blockchain or any other individual technology. Trust Computing denotes the evaluation of trust as a computable outcome of explicitly verified conditions on identity, authority, collective approval, policy, and lifecycle. Within this perspective, Trusted Computing is treated as a complementary component, since Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-supported isolation for security-sensitive computation, and remote attestation can provide evidence of the integrity of the execution environment [23, 17]. Nevertheless, Trusted Computing does not by itself determine the correctness of an authorisation policy. Consequently, the current stage concentrates on the authorisation conditions themselves, and hardware-assisted trusted execution is left for future work.

text: Identity concerns whether a participant can be reliably identified. Authority concerns whether that participant possesses the relevant role or permission to participate in a particular decision. Multi-party authorisation concerns whether the required threshold of independently verified participants has jointly established the authorisation condition. Policy compliance concerns whether the requested access is consistent with the authorised purpose and data scope. Consent is instead treated as a structured and trust-aware authorisation object, C = (I, A, P, T, L, E), that connects the relevant participants, authority requirements, policy constraints, temporal and jurisdictional conditions, and evidence associated with an authorisation decision.

text: Systematic Literature Review

The objective of the review is to examine how existing approaches address conditions required for a trustworthy authorisation decision and where gaps remain. Healthcare research has emphasised informed consent [31, 14, 24, 22, 12]. Multi-party trust research has investigated decentralised consent management [2, 7, 3, 30, 26]. Research on decentralised identity has developed mechanisms for credential verification [20, 33, 4, 16, 5, 27]. Access-control research has investigated role-based approaches [32, 11, 28, 25]. However, these mechanisms are commonly developed and evaluated as separate components.

text: Key Requirements for Trustworthy Multi-Party Consent Authorisation

A healthcare consent decision passes through specification and approval, enforcement at each data-access request, and maintenance or withdrawal over time. The six requirements below cover these phases, and each corresponds to one sub-research question of Section 3.

items: **Req 1: Representation of consent as an evaluable authorisation object.** Consent should be represented as an evaluable authorisation object rather than as a database entry or blockchain transaction. Its identities, authority requirements, purpose and data scope, temporal validity, jurisdiction, and evidence should each be evaluable at every request.

**Req 2: Decentralised verification of identity and authority.** Participants should be identifiable without a central identity provider. Identity verification establishes who is participating, while authority verification determines whether that entity satisfies the requirements associated with a particular consent.

**Req 3: Multi-party authorisation through a verifiable threshold.** A predefined number of designated parties should each provide an independently verifiable approval, recorded in the consent object and checkable later.

**Req 4: Policy- and context-aware enforcement at the time of access.** The access decision must be evaluated against the purpose and data-scope constraints explicitly associated with the consent. Every request should also be evaluated against contextual constraints such as jurisdiction, because many unauthorised disclosures are caused by legitimate requesters who exceed their scope [11].

**Req 5: Temporal validity and lifecycle control of consent.** The validity interval should be enforced at every request, revocation should be immediate and verifiable, and only controlled lifecycle transitions should be permitted.

**Req 6: Verifiable auditability and security assurance.** Every decision should leave independently verifiable evidence, and security properties should be validated formally or through systematic adversarial testing. A system may execute valid authorisation scenarios without demonstrating that invalid identities, insufficient approvals, or policy violations cannot produce an unintended access decision.

Questions 1 to 5 of the seven review questions correspond to Req 1 to Req 5, while Questions 6 and 7 together correspond to Req 6.

text: Review of the Six Streams

Each included study was assigned to the stream on which it is coded most strongly. **Consent representation and blockchain-based consent governance (Req 1).** Both studies of this stream are deployed platforms graded Partial. Soohoo et al. [67] describe the iAgree portal across three United States health systems with a permissioned Ethereum audit contract, but consent enforcement is outside its scope. Tremper et al. [72] report ten years of the Mainzelliste service with FHIR consent directives, but specify no check semantics and no demonstrated enforcement of withdrawal. Neither study involves more than one authorising party, and the supporting references treat consent as a boolean grant [36, 60] or as conditions fixed at encryption time [70, 78].

Research Gap

The systematic literature review indicates that substantial research has been conducted on individual mechanisms for securing healthcare data sharing. They are commonly investigated as independent technical solutions rather than as coordinated components of a unified trust-oriented authorisation model. The few studies that coordinate several of them in one decision [58, 61, 45, 66, 57] do not make multi-party approval a standing condition of that decision, and they do not assure the conjunction formally or empirically.

text: The central gap is therefore not the absence of technologies for recording consent, verifying identity, or restricting data access. Rather, it is the absence of a sufficiently integrated model explaining how these mechanisms collectively establish a trustworthy authorisation decision. text: Main Research Question

Based on the identified research gap, the overarching research question is formulated as follows: **"How can a trust-oriented computing framework establish and enforce trustworthy multi-party consent for decentralised healthcare data sharing under identity, authority, and policy constraints?"** The formulation of this question deliberately emphasises trust-oriented computing rather than any individual implementation technology. Establishment concerns how trustworthy participants, authority relationships, and collective consent decisions are created. Enforcement concerns how these established conditions are evaluated when a healthcare data-access request is made.

text: RO1: Trust-Centric Consent Model

The first research objective is to develop a trust-aware consent model that represents patient consent as a structured and evaluable authorisation object. text: Research Architecture: MVC

The proposed research architecture adopts a Model–View–Controller (MVC) design to provide a structured implementation foundation for the trusted multi-party consent management framework. Within the proposed framework, MVC is extended to support a more fundamental separation between the representation of consent, the interaction of independent stakeholders, and the enforcement of security-critical authorisation decisions. A healthcare consent decision may involve patients, guardians, healthcare professionals, and auditors, each of whom may possess different identities, authorities, and responsibilities. Consequently, the system cannot rely on a single user authentication event or a static permission entry to determine whether access should be granted. Instead, the authorisation decision must emerge from the coordinated evaluation of independently verifiable security conditions.

At the highest level, the architecture consists of three complementary layers. The View Layer represents the interaction boundary with independent healthcare stakeholders. The Controller Layer represents the security decision and coordination boundary. The Model Layer represents the persistent trust, consent, policy, and authorisation state. {F6} illustrates the conceptual relationship among these layers. The protected healthcare data are deliberately positioned outside the three MVC layers as a protected resource whose access is mediated by the Controller rather than directly exposed to the View.

text: Trust Evaluation and Architectural Boundaries

The architectural layers cooperate through a controlled authorisation sequence rather than through unrestricted direct communication. As illustrated in {F8}, the Controller coordinates a sequence of trust predicates representing the conditions established by the sub-research questions. The first condition, V~I~(u), determines whether the requesting participant possesses valid identity and authority evidence. The second condition, V~A~(C), determines whether the required independently verified participants have collectively satisfied the authorisation threshold N. The third condition, V~P~(C, R), determines whether the requested operation complies with the consent policy, including purpose and data-scope restrictions. The fourth condition, V~T~(C, t), determines whether the consent remains valid at the time of the request. The fifth condition, V~L~(C), determines whether the recorded jurisdictional constraint of the consent is satisfied. Lifecycle validity and revocation are evaluated within V~A~ rather than within V~L~. The integrated decision can therefore be expressed as {E22}.

The MVC architecture also provides a direct implementation structure for the research objectives, as summarised in {T13}. text: Trust-Aware Consent Creation Procedure and Algorithm

The procedure establishes a valid and auditable consent object by sequentially validating the participating entities, consent purpose, data scope, and temporal constraints. The system first validates the patient's identity I~p~. If I~p~ cannot be validated, the procedure terminates and returns REJECT. The system validates the designated doctor D and the guardian set G. This step prevents an arbitrary third party from being treated as an authorised representative of the patient. The intended data-use purpose P~u~ is validated and bound to the consent object so that authorisation is not interpreted as unrestricted access to the patient's healthcare information. The requested data scope S~C~ is validated to determine which healthcare resources may be accessed under the consent. This step establishes the principle of least privilege by ensuring that consent is associated with explicitly defined data resources rather than the patient's entire healthcare record.

text: Procedure for Threshold-Based Multi-Party Authorisation

The procedure determines whether a consent-defined authorisation requirement has received sufficient valid approvals from the designated participants. The system first retrieves the required participant set G associated with the consent object C. The threshold N must satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ |G|. The approval a is not considered valid until the identity and authority of the submitting participant have been verified. The verification process may invoke the DID and VC verification procedure described in {A2}. If the verification fails, the approval is classified as invalid. The system records the invalid approval event and returns DENY for that approval attempt.

Status: Done

This section presents the solution to RQ4, which is addressed by RO4. The objective is to ensure that an otherwise valid requester cannot access healthcare information outside the purpose and data scope authorised by the consent. RO4 develops a policy-aware access-control mechanism capable of evaluating purpose and data-scope constraints before an access decision is issued. A valid identity and sufficient approval do not necessarily imply that every requested operation is permitted, since, for example, a legitimate doctor with a valid consent may request data beyond the authorised scope, or for a purpose that does not match the one specified by the patient.

text: The Proposed Solution for RQ6
Status: Partially completed (for RQ1 to RQ4)

RO6 addresses RQ6 by formally analysing and empirically evaluating whether the proposed trust-oriented authorisation framework satisfies its defined security and authorisation properties. The objective combines two complementary forms of assurance. Formal security assurance specifies the conditions under which the authorisation mechanism should be considered secure and consistent. Empirical validation evaluates whether the implemented system behaves according to those conditions. The scenario-based empirical half has been carried out on the HALAH prototype for RQ1 to RQ4, together with the temporal and revocation controls of RQ5, whereas the formal assurance and the full evaluation remain for CA3.

text: The HALAH Prototype and Live Scenarios

The HALAH (History Access Link for Authorised Healthcare) prototype is a role-based consent management platform with separate patient, guardian, doctor, and auditor interfaces. Its consent token contract, ConsentSBTv3, was compiled in Remix and deployed to Sepolia through MetaMask as a soulbound ERC-721 token, so transfers between accounts are blocked. Each token stores the pseudonymous patient and requester addresses, a hash of the purpose, the validity window, a two-letter jurisdiction code, and a revocation flag. No medical content is written to the chain, although the plaintext purpose is passed as a parameter of the mint transaction and is therefore visible in the public transaction input. All medical records used in the demonstration are synthetic and derived from the Synthea dataset.

text: Unit-Level Adversarial Tests

The adversarial tests assume honest infrastructure and exercise the decision functions, the proof verifier, the digest function of the audit ledger, and the contract at unit level. The adversary, whether an outside requester or a participant of the consent, tries to obtain or keep access without satisfying a condition of C, or to alter the anchored consent or the recorded evidence of a decision. It can supply crafted inputs to the decision functions, alter the bits of a Groth16 proof or its public signals, and send transactions to the contract from an account that is not its owner. Several capabilities are outside the scope of this evaluation, because the prototype does not defend against them. For example, the interface authenticates no role, and each guardian signing key is derived from the public guardian DID. The adversary is also assumed to have no write access to the stores, apart from rewriting an audit event, and no control of the server clock.

text: The evaluation has six limitations. First, A12 runs the contract source on an in-memory Ethereum virtual machine, so it does not show the behaviour of the deployed bytecode. Second, the SHA-256 digest of the audit ledger is neither keyed nor chained, so the ledger is not tamper-evident against a party with write access to the store. Third, the signed guardian message covers only the consent identifier, the guardian, and the network, so a change of scope, purpose, requester, expiry, or jurisdiction after approval is not detected. Fourth, A6 relies on the server clock, A7 on the jurisdiction declared by the requester, and A8 on the revocation flag of the local store. Fifth, the Groth16 result holds under a single-party development trusted setup, with the prover and the verifier on the same server. Sixth, the measurements come from a single container and five transactions, so they are indicative only. These tests are not a penetration test of the deployed system.
